name: Ngizim
catalog_citation: Schuh, Russell G. 1981. A Dictionary of Ngizim. University of California Publications in Linguistics 99. Berkeley: University of California Press. (archive.org item schuh-a-dictionary-of-ngizim-1981, djvu text layer)
catalog_locator: Introduction sec. 1.3 'Tones', pp. xiii-xiv; footnote 2 to sec. 2 (verbs) on tone predictability
catalog_quote: 1.3. Tones. Syllables carry one of the following phonetic tones: ... high ... low ... downstep ... falling ... rising ... extra high (found only on certain phonaesthetic words) ... Ngizim may be analyzed as having only two phonemic tones, high and low (but see the remark on downstep immediately below). The contour tones (falling and rising) may be analyzed as sequences of high-low and low-high on single syllables respectively. Downstep is the result of the loss of a low tone between two highs where the second high is slightly lower than the first because of the universal Chadic downdrift phenomenon. ... Whereas falling tones and downsteps are not uncommon in lexical items, rising tones are very rare and seem to be almost totally restricted to final syllables where a final vowel has been truncated

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding passage (Schuh 1981 sec. 1.3 'Tones', pp. xiii-xiv) and footnote 2 are present verbatim in the held archive.org text layer at the stated place; only scanned hyphenation and elided tone-mark glyphs differ. (2) Deciding source is a dictionary introduction (1981) by the language's sole major describer; it is a sketch, but I fetched sources and read the Glottolog 'grammar' (Schuh 1972 dissertation, phonological sketch pp. 11-12), Schuh's 2002 tone handout (Handout 04), a text-layer copy of Schuh 1978 SAL, and the 2009 YLRP dictionary introduction: all describe Ngizim prosody exclusively as a two-tone (H/L) system with downstep/downdrift, contour tones as HL/LH sequences, low functional load of tone; none states any word-stress or accent rule, and the only 'stress' tokens across ~700 pp are English usages. sources.citation: Schuh, Russell G. 1972. Aspects of Ngizim Syntax. PhD dissertation, UCLA. xix+487 pp. (Glottolog hhtype grammar; author's scan from his UCLA Papers page via Wayback)
sources.quote: 'Ngizim has two phonemic tones, Hi and Lo. Phonetic Falling and Rising tones are respectively sequences of Hi-Lo and Lo-Hi on a single syllable. A Downstep is always analyzable as a Hi following a Hi-Lo sequence where the Lo has been suppressed... While minimal tone pairs exist in both nouns and verbs, tone carries a low functional load in Ngizim.' Sec. 1.2 'Tone Classes': 'Verbs are lexically high or low tone. sources.citation: Schuh, Russell G. (ed.) 2009. Ngizim-English-Hausa Dictionary, 2nd edition, compiled by Ahmed Mohammed Bedu, Joseph Ya'u Yakubu, Mohammed Alhaji Adamu, Usman Babayo Garba. Potiskum: Yobe Languages Research Project. 175 pp.
sources.quote: 'The distinctions between long and short vowels and distinctions between tones (whether a syllable is spoken with a higher or lower voice pitch) are both important for correct pronunciation and for distinguishing the meanings of words in Ngizim... LOW TONES have a grave accent, HIGH TONES have no accent marks, FALLING TONES have a circumflex accent, and RISING TONES, which are rare, have a hachek... It is not clear, however, whether downstep is a distinctive tone of Ngizim or a variant of high tone at the end of a phrase after another high.' No mention of stress.

sources.citation: Schuh, Russell G. 2002. Handout 04, 'Bade/Ngizim Tones: Tone System, Tone Rules, Morphologically Conditioned Tones'. Linguistics 252 (Bade/Ngizim Phonology and Morphology), UCLA, Winter 2002. 20 pp.
sources.quote: p.1: 'Like all Chadic languages, languages of the Bade/Ngizim group are tone languages... TWO LEVEL TONES AND DOWNDRIFT INTONATION... On heavy syllables, Fall is probably analyzable as Hi!Lo on one syllable... RISING contour throughout the language group seems to be restricted to monosyllables beginning in a voiced obstruent... LOW FUNCTIONAL LOAD OF TONE.' p.12: Hyman (1975 letter) on Western Bade recordings: 'your downsteps... really indicate increases/decreases in intensity and duration... sources.citation: Schuh, Russell G. 1978. Bade/Ngizim vowels and syllable structure. Studies in African Linguistics 9(3): 247-283. (text-layer copy from SAL open-access full issue; held copy was image-only)
sources.quote: Paper is about schwa placement, consonant-sequence constraints and syllabification; tone enters only as marking conventions (fn. 2: acute = high, grave = low, circumflex = falling, tick = downstep) and as a conditioning factor for Bade prothesis. The only 'stress' tokens are the English verb ('I should stress here'). Silent on word stress.
sources.locator: pp. 247-283 (issue txt lines 119-1624; extracted to); fn. 2 p. 247 tone-marking conventions

sources.citation: Newman, Roxana Ma. 2006[?]. Russell G. Schuh: A biographical profile and bibliography. Studies in African Linguistics (Schuh festschrift issue). 16 pp.
sources.quote: Bibliographic only: enumerates Schuh's Ngizim works (1971 verb forms, 1977 determiners, 1978 vowels/syllables, 1981 dictionary, 1982 focus, 2003 Kanuri influence, 2004 Ngizim-English-Hausa dictionary); no dedicated Ngizim tone/prosody monograph exists in his output. Used to judge best-available, not for a stress statement.
